levels.title: Read First, Learn Later
levels.story: Wren shows Kit two apprentices. One reads every book in the old archive for years, then learns a new craft in a week. The other starts the craft cold. "Who finishes first?" asks Wren. "The one who read first," says Kit.

everyday.scene: A new employee who has read widely picks up a new job faster than someone starting from nothing.
everyday.question: Could a program do the same: read a huge amount first, and then learn a specific job quickly?
everyday.answer: Yes. It is first trained on huge amounts of raw text, then trained a little more on its real job. This two-step approach is how most modern language models are built.

lessons.title: Learning from raw text
text: Pretraining teaches a model language before it is given a job. It reads enormous amounts of raw text and learns to guess missing or next words. The right answers come from the text itself, so no one has to label anything.
This is called self-supervised learning: the training goal is worked out automatically from the inputs. Two common goals are guessing the next word and guessing a word that has been hidden.

terms.meaning: Training on huge amounts of raw text before a specific job.
The right answers are taken from the data itself.

references.title: Hugging Face LLM course: How do Transformers work?

lessons.title: Hiding words
text: BERT, a model from Google published in 2018, was pretrained by hiding words. In its masked language modelling task, 15 percent of tokens are picked at random for a prediction task, and the model must guess them from the words around them.
In a 40-token text that is 6 tokens. The model can use words on both sides of a gap, so it learns to read context from both directions.

lessons.title: Then fine-tune

text.text: After pretraining, the model is trained a little more on the real job, such as sorting reviews. This second step is called fine-tuning. It takes only a small amount of extra training, because pretraining has already taught the model a lot about language.

text: This is an example of transfer learning: knowledge from one task is reused to help with a related one. Sharing pretrained models also saves the cost of training every model from the start.

deeper.title: Not always a win
text: Pretraining usually helps, but not always. One 2020 study reported that pretraining can hurt accuracy in some cases, which led its authors to suggest self-training instead.

fieldNotes.title: Self-supervised learning
fieldNotes.text: Many popular language models are trained on large amounts of raw text in a self-supervised way, where the training goal is computed automatically from the inputs.

source.title: Hugging Face LLM course: How do Transformers work?

fieldNotes.title: BERT
fieldNotes.text: BERT is a language model developed at Google AI and published in 2018. It is pretrained with masked language modelling and then fine-tuned for specific tasks.

fieldNotes.title: Transfer learning
fieldNotes.text: Transfer learning reuses knowledge learned on one task to boost performance on a related task.

summary: You saw how a model learns from raw text by guessing hidden words, then adapts to a job with a small labelled set. That two-step recipe is behind most modern language models.
Wren shuts the old archive door. "Read widely first. Then learn the craft."

mistake.title: Thinking pretraining needs labels
mistake.text: Pretraining uses the text itself for answers, which is why it can use huge amounts of text. The labels are only needed for the small fine-tuning step.
